speaker: recall
text: {mAgo}, {mWhere}, you went with {mOther} instead of me. You said, and I wrote it down: “{mQuote}.” I haven’t mentioned it since. I’m mentioning it now.
variants: {mAgo}, {mWhere}, you went with {mOther} instead of me. You said, and I wrote it down: “{mQuote}.” I haven’t mentioned it since. I’m mentioning it now.
You remember. {mAgo}, {mWhere}: “{mQuote}.” {mOther} looked very pleased. I have thought about {mOther}’s face a great deal since.
People still bring it up. “Weren’t you the one {title} overruled for {mOther}?” That was {mAgo}. I’d like it to stop being the thing I’m known for.

choices.label: I shouldn’t have done it in front of everyone.
choices.reaction: {speaker} accepts the apology formally, then informally, then formally again for the minutes.

choices.label: {mOther} had the better idea.
choices.hint: Stand by it · The grudge deepens
choices.reaction: {speaker} nods slowly. {mOther} hears about it within the hour and becomes, briefly, unbearable.

speaker: recall
text: Ever since you sided with {mOther}, {mAgo}, {mOther} has been unbearable. There’s a lanyard now. {mOther} had it made.
variants: Ever since you sided with {mOther}, {mAgo}, {mOther} has been unbearable. There’s a lanyard now. {mOther} had it made.
{mOther} keeps quoting you. “{mQuote}.” At breakfast. At the {meeting}. Once, at a funeral. You chose {mOther} over me, and I live with the consequences daily.

choices.label: I’ll have a word with {mOther}.
choices.reaction: The lanyard is retired. {mOther} keeps it in a drawer and looks at it sometimes.

choices.label: {mOther} earned it.
choices.reaction: {speaker} commissions a larger lanyard. A lanyard arms race begins.

speaker: agnes
text: I am compiling the year’s minutes. Under “Things {title} Said”, I have: “{mQuote}”, said to {mWho} {mWhen}, {mWhere}. Do you stand by it? I ask because it will be bound.

choices.label: Every word.
choices.reaction: Agnes binds it in green cloth. {mWho} is given a copy, which they did not ask for.

choices.label: Strike it from the record.
choices.reaction: Agnes strikes it out with a single, perfect line. The line is itself minuted.

speaker: recall
text: {mAgo} I asked for something, and you said: “{mQuote}.” I’ve since been proven right. I won’t say how. I would simply like it noted.

choices.label: Noted. You were right.
choices.reaction: {speaker} has the word “noted” embroidered on a cushion, and brings the cushion to the {meeting}.

choices.label: Noted that you’re keeping score.
choices.reaction: {speaker} writes “keeping score” on the list, which is now a scorecard.

speaker: recall
text: {mAgo} you said: “{mQuote}.” It meant a great deal. So I’ve gone ahead and done eleven more things in the same spirit. I assumed you’d want that. Here is the list.

choices.label: Wonderful. Carry on.
choices.reaction: {speaker} carries on. Items twelve to nineteen are added by lunchtime.

choices.label: That was one decision, not a mandate.
choices.reaction: {speaker} folds the list very small. You later find it, unfolded again, pinned to the noticeboard.

speaker: recall
text: {mAgo} I was proven right, and you said so: “{mQuote}.” Privately. Which I appreciate. But the people who laughed at me laughed at the {meeting}. Would you say it there?

choices.label: I’ll say it at the {meeting}.
choices.hint: Public credit · Someone else is embarrassed
choices.reaction: You say it. The room applauds. {speaker} pretends not to have prepared a response, then delivers it.

choices.label: It doesn’t need saying twice.
choices.reaction: {speaker} says that’s fine, in the voice people use when it is not fine.

speaker: martin
text: There’s a fire inspector at the door. Unannounced. He wants our evacuation plan. We have one: I laminated it in week two, mostly because I wanted to try the new orange pouches. Everyone laughed. May I show him?

choices.label: Show him Martin’s plan.
choices.reaction: The inspector calls it the best plan he has seen in a community setting. Martin is asked to laminate the inspector’s plans too.

choices.label: I’ll handle this myself.
choices.reaction: You improvise. The inspector writes eleven things down. The fine arrives on very thin paper. Martin offers to laminate it.

speaker: dez
text: Small update. On local radio this morning I may have promised that the weather presenter from Channel Four will be at our next {meeting}. I haven’t asked her. But I said it with total confidence, which is half the battle.

choices.label: Then we’d better be ready for her.
choices.reaction: Chairs are added. Someone irons a tablecloth. Dez practises a handshake that is both warm and meteorological.

choices.label: Call the station and retract it.
choices.reaction: The station reads your retraction on air. Dez listens in the car with the engine running and doesn’t come in for a while.

speaker: gary
text: She came. The weather presenter. Not because of Dez: she saw my whale flyer in the library and thought this was a whale-watching group. She stayed for the soup. She’d like to join. She knows a lot about whales.

choices.label: Welcome her. Let Dez take the credit.
choices.reaction: Dez accepts the credit with grace and a short speech. Gary nods. He knows. The whales know.

choices.label: Credit where due: Gary’s flyer.
choices.reaction: Gary gets a round of applause and immediately falls asleep, overwhelmed. Dez applauds loudest, slightly hurt.

speaker: dez
text: She didn’t come. I told everyone she sent her regards. Then people asked what her regards were, so I’ve been writing them. There are quite a lot of regards now. Some of them are forecasts.

choices.label: Come clean at the {meeting}.
choices.reaction: Dez confesses. The room forgives him instantly. Someone asks whether the forecasts were accurate. Two were.

choices.label: Keep the regards coming.
choices.reaction: “Regards from the Weather” becomes a regular feature of the newsletter. It is, by some distance, the most popular one.

speaker: priya
text: The council votes on our hall booking at three o’clock today. I’ve also organised a picnic at three o’clock, because it’s the first sunny day in five weeks and everyone is exhausted. I think the picnic matters more. I know how that sounds.

choices.label: Everyone to the council.
choices.reaction: The booking is approved. Priya eats the picnic alone in the park and reports that it was, honestly, a very good picnic.

choices.label: Everyone to the picnic.
choices.hint: Joy · Lose the hall for a while
choices.reaction: The council gives the hall to the Knitting Circle. Nobody at the picnic finds out until five, and nobody minds until six.

speaker: martin
text: We lost the hall. This week’s {meeting} is in the bus shelter. I want to be cross about the picnic, {title}. I can’t. It was the best day we’ve had. That’s the problem. It was a lovely problem.

choices.label: Book somewhere for next week.
choices.reaction: Martin books a scout hut and laminates directions to it. Several people still go to the bus shelter, out of affection.

choices.label: The bus shelter has its charms.
choices.reaction: Passengers start staying for the {meeting}. Two miss their bus on purpose. One joins.

speaker: agnes
text: Before anyone votes on fixing the roof, every member must re-read the founding minutes. It is the only way to be sure the roof is consistent with our principles. At current reading speeds this will take eleven weeks. The roof is leaking now. I am aware.

choices.label: The minutes first.
choices.reaction: Members read the minutes under umbrellas. Comprehension is high. So is the damp.

choices.label: Fix the roof. Read later.
choices.reaction: The roof is fixed in an afternoon. Agnes notes in the minutes that the roof is now “unprincipled, but dry”.

speaker: gary
text: My whale newsletter went to the wrong mailing list. Forty marine biologists have joined. They think we’re about whales. I haven’t told them. I’m not completely sure we aren’t.

choices.label: We are, in a sense, about whales.
choices.reaction: The biologists are delighted. Gary becomes, informally, Head of Whales. Nobody objects, because nobody is sure it wasn’t already true.

choices.label: Gently explain the mix-up.
choices.reaction: Most of the biologists leave politely. Eight stay. Whales or no whales, they say, the soup is excellent.

text: The biologists have a question. What is {movement}’s official position on whales? We have drafted one. It is supportive. It is forty pages. {c.gary} has read it twice and cried once.

choices.label: Adopt it.
choices.reaction: {Movement} now has a position on whales. It is more detailed than its position on anything else.

choices.label: We have no position on whales.
choices.reaction: Fifteen biologists leave. Gary is quiet for a week, then puts up a small, unofficial whale on the noticeboard.

speaker: rolf
text: The misprinted mugs, the ones where the logo came out looking like a worried potato. I was going to write them off. They’ve sold out. People love the potato. I don’t understand why, and I do not enjoy not understanding why.

choices.label: Lean into the potato.
choices.reaction: The worried potato appears on tea towels and badges. Members adopt it as a sort of mascot; it unites people in a way the logo never did. Rolf calls it “the most profitable mistake of my career”, with visible discomfort.

choices.label: Reprint them properly.
choices.reaction: The corrected mugs sell four. Rolf keeps one potato mug on his desk, as a warning.

speaker: lionel
text: My Department of Departments has no clear function. I accept that. However, while auditing itself it noticed that the hall is double-booked for the {meeting}: by us, and by a wedding. The wedding is in six days.

choices.label: Thank the Department of Departments.
choices.reaction: The booking is untangled. The Department of Departments receives a commendation, which it files in a department created for the purpose.

choices.label: Merge the {meeting} with the wedding.
choices.reaction: The bride is surprised. The groom joins. The speeches mention {belief} more than either family expected.

speaker: martin
text: Membership cards! Numbered, laminated, with a little photo of each member looking their best. Everyone loves a card. I’ve got the laminator warming up and a queue already forming.

choices.label: Cards at the door.
choices.reaction: Everyone gets a card. The queue at the door reaches the bus stop, where three people waiting to join give up and go home.

choices.label: Leave the door open.
choices.reaction: The door stays open. Martin laminates a single card, his own, and shows it to people who don’t ask.

speaker: dez
text: I promised the mayor a parade. This Saturday. We don’t have a parade. But the carnival is on Saturday, and if we walk in front of it confidently enough, I believe we become the front of the carnival.

choices.label: Walk in front of the carnival.
choices.reaction: It works. Thirty thousand people cheer you for eleven minutes before anyone checks the programme. The carnival’s collection buckets end up with you. The paper calls you “the surprise opening act”.

choices.label: Tell the mayor the truth.
choices.reaction: The mayor is relieved; she had also promised a parade, to someone else. Dez is quiet for an entire afternoon.

speaker: ophelia
text: Every branch meets on a different night. It’s chaos for the newsletter, the radio show and me. One night, everywhere. It’s efficient, it’s fair, and I’ve already printed the calendars.

choices.label: One night, everywhere.
choices.reaction: The calendars are beautiful. In nine towns, the people who could only come on the old night stop coming. Nobody notices for a month.

choices.label: Let each branch choose.
choices.reaction: Ophelia reprints the calendars with forty-one different nights on them. They are still beautiful.

speaker: rolf
text: We need a proper external auditor. Not because anything is wrong. Because one day something will be, and I want it found by a professional. The good ones charge by the hour. They have a lot of hours.

choices.label: Hire the auditor.
choices.reaction: The auditor finds nothing wrong, very thoroughly, over six weeks. The invoice is the largest thing the movement has ever bought. Rolf frames the clean report.

choices.label: Rolf can audit us himself.
choices.reaction: Rolf audits himself and finds two biscuits unaccounted for. He reports himself to himself and is, reluctantly, cleared.

speaker: recall
text: I’m done, {title}. It wasn’t one thing. Well. It was mostly one thing: {mAgo}, {mWhere}, “{mQuote}.” {exit}

choices.label: Stay. Tell me what it would take.
choices.reaction: {speaker} stays. It isn’t fixed. But for now it isn’t broken either, and you both know which of you has to be careful.

choices.label: I understand. Go well.
choices.reaction: {speaker} goes. The {meeting} is quieter afterwards, in a way nobody mentions and everybody notices.

speaker: any
text: I’m done, {title}. It wasn’t one thing. It was a hundred small things, and you were there for all of them. {exit}

choices.label: Stay. Tell me what it would take.
choices.reaction: {speaker} stays. It isn’t fixed. But for now it isn’t broken either, and you both know which of you has to be careful.

choices.label: I understand. Go well.
choices.reaction: {speaker} goes. The {meeting} is quieter afterwards, in a way nobody mentions and everybody notices.

speaker: any
text: Nobody {departedHabit} anymore. Since {departed} left, the {meeting} finishes on time, and nobody can explain why that feels worse.
variants: Nobody {departedHabit} anymore. Since {departed} left, the {meeting} finishes on time, and nobody can explain why that feels worse.
A newcomer asked who used to sit in that chair. I said {departed}. They asked what {departed} was like. I said: someone who {departedHabit}. Then I had to go outside for a bit.
I saw {departed} at the bus stop. We talked about the weather for nine minutes. Neither of us mentioned {movement}. It was the longest conversation about {movement} I’ve ever had.

choices.label: Reach out to {departed}.
choices.reaction: You write a short note. You rewrite it four times. The fifth version just says “The door’s open.”

choices.label: We manage without them.
choices.reaction: You manage. Someone else starts doing it, slightly wrong, and that becomes the new way.

speaker: departed
text: I got your note. I’m not saying I’d come back. I’m saying I walked past the {meeting} twice last week, and nobody was doing it properly.

choices.label: Come back. On your terms.
choices.reaction: {speaker} comes back. By the second {meeting} it’s as if they never left, which is both the good news and the bad news.

choices.label: It’s better this way.
choices.reaction: {speaker} nods, as if they’d expected it, and gives you back the key they forgot to return.

speaker: bev
text: Hello, love. Bev. I’ve been watching your lot wander about. Gary went to the wrong town twice last week, and one of them doesn’t exist. Give me the rota. I’ll have everyone where they’re needed by {day}, and home when they need to be.

choices.label: The rota is yours, Bev.
choices.hint: A scheduler · You set the focus
choices.reaction: Bev pins a rota to the fridge. By the end of the day everyone knows where they’re going, what they’re taking, and that there will be sandwiches.

choices.label: We like the chaos, thanks.
choices.hint: Everyone keeps going where they like
choices.reaction: Bev says “suit yourself” in a tone that makes it clear she’ll be back. She leaves you a sandwich anyway.

speaker: bev
text: Me again. Dez has opened four towns this month and paid for the petrol with the biscuit tin. Priya’s been in the same town so long they’ve given her a key to it. I’m only saying. The offer stands.

choices.label: All right, Bev. Take the rota.
choices.hint: A scheduler · You set the focus
choices.reaction: Bev takes the rota, the biscuit tin and Dez’s car keys, in that order.

choices.label: Still chaos, Bev.
choices.reaction: Bev nods. She adds you to her own private rota, under “ones to keep an eye on”.

speaker: bev
text: Everyone I send out gets a sandwich. It’s not in the budget. It’s in my handbag. The handbag is getting very heavy, love. Can the sandwiches be in the budget?

choices.label: Sandwiches are in the budget.
choices.reaction: The Sandwich Line is added to the accounts. Recruitment rises in every town, which Bev attributes entirely to egg and cress.

choices.label: The handbag has been working well.
choices.reaction: Bev buys a bigger handbag. It has wheels. It becomes, in its way, famous.

speaker: bev
text: I’ve worked out a route for Gary where he can sleep on the bus between towns. He arrives everywhere refreshed. He has also, without waking up, recruited eleven bus drivers.

choices.label: Keep Gary on the bus.
choices.reaction: Gary becomes the movement’s travelling ambassador, mostly horizontal. The bus drivers start a branch that only meets at terminuses.

choices.label: Gary should be awake for some of it.
choices.reaction: Gary tries. He stays awake for a whole route, waves at everyone, and recruits nine people and a dog. Then he sleeps for two days.

speaker: bev
text: Dez has spent the petrol money opening another town nobody asked him to open. The town is delighted, mind. They’ve given him a sash. I need a ruling, love: does Dez get a petrol budget, or does Dez walk?

choices.label: Give Dez a proper petrol budget.
choices.reaction: Dez receives a petrol budget and a laminated map from Martin. He opens two towns that week and sends Bev a postcard from each.

choices.label: Dez walks.
choices.reaction: Dez walks. He walks surprisingly far. He opens a town on foot and arrives so tired and sincere that they make him an honorary citizen.

speaker: bev
text: There’s a man from the paper outside the garage with a long lens, and everyone’s knackered. I’d like to give the whole lot of them a week off. Not a holiday. A lie-down. The papers can’t write about people having a lie-down.

choices.label: A week off for everyone.
choices.reaction: Bev sends everyone home with a sandwich. The man with the long lens photographs a week of closed curtains and gives up.

choices.label: Keep everyone working.
choices.reaction: Bev says “on your head be it” and hands out the rota, and a spare sandwich for the man with the long lens.
